title: Wigner symmetries single out symmetric Wasserstein distances in all finite dimensions
abstract: We study the quantum Wasserstein distances introduced by De Palma and Trevisan associated with quadratic cost operators generated by families of self-adjoint observables. We first show that an arbitrary positive semidefinite cost operator is completely determined by the restriction of the corresponding Wasserstein distance to pairs of pure states. This allows geometric invariance of the pure-state distance to be translated directly into invariance of the cost operator.   Within the class of nonzero quadratic costs generated by at most $d^2-1$ observables on a $d$-dimensional Hilbert space, we prove that the Wasserstein isometry monoid consists exactly of the Wigner symmetries, that is, unitary and antiunitary conjugations, if and only if the distance is invariant under unitary conjugations on pure states. Equivalently, the cost operator intertwines the adjoint representation of the unitary group and is a positive scalar multiple of the identity on the traceless subspace.   We further construct explicit mutually inverse maps between quadratic cost operators generated by observables and Hilbert--Schmidt frame-type operators formed from their traceless parts. Under this correspondence, isotropy of the cost is equivalent to the tight frame property of the associated Hilbert--Schmidt operator. Consequently, a nonzero isotropic cost requires at least $d^2-1$ self-adjoint generators, and equality holds precisely when their traceless parts form, up to a common scale, a Hilbert--Schmidt orthonormal basis. Thus the geometric, representation-theoretic, operator-theoretic, and frame-theoretic notions of symmetry all determine the same one-parameter family of quantum Wasserstein distances.
summary: This paper rigorously characterizes symmetric quantum Wasserstein distances on finite-dimensional Hilbert spaces. It proves that multiple seemingly disparate symmetry conditions—including isometry group structure, representation invariance, and frame properties—are all equivalent ways of defining the same specific distance metric. This unifies several advanced mathematical tools to understand the geometry of quantum state space.
main_problem: The core problem is characterizing quantum Wasserstein distances whose isometry group is precisely the Wigner symmetries (unitary/antiunitary conjugations).
main_result: Multiple mathematical notions of symmetry—geometric, representation-theoretic, operator-theoretic, and frame-theoretic—are proven to be equivalent conditions that characterize these specific symmetric quantum Wasserstein distances.
method: The analysis involves translating geometric invariance (isometries) into algebraic constraints on the cost operator, utilizing concepts from group representations (adjoint action) and frame theory (tight frames).
model_or_system: The study is set in finite-dimensional complex Hilbert spaces ($\mathcal{H}$ of dimension $d$), focusing on quantum states represented by density operators $ho$ and distances defined via quadratic cost operators $C_A$ associated with self-adjoint observables $\{A_k\}$.
key_observables: Quantum Wasserstein distance ($D_A$), the quadratic cost operator ($C_A$), and the traceless parts of observables ($\pi_0(A)$).
important_parameters: The dimension $d$ of the Hilbert space, and the number of generating observables $K$, which is constrained to be at most $d^2-1$.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the existence of a specific structure for the cost operator (e.g., being isotropic or generated by observables) to establish the equivalence theorems.

paper_structure: The paper builds from establishing basic formalism (Dirac notation), moving through representation theory (adjoint actions) to prove a central theorem that equates six different symmetry conditions for the quantum Wasserstein distance.
why_interesting: This work provides deep mathematical structure to optimal transport in quantum mechanics, linking fundamental symmetries of quantum evolution (Wigner symmetries) directly to the geometry of state spaces defined by generalized distances.
